content: Monitoring and assessment are essential components of reducing surgical site infections (SSIs) and are already integrated into routine practices in many countries. These activities include evaluating and providing feedback on both the processes and outcomes related to SSI prevention. Within a multimodal improvement strategy, the examples provided here emphasize process evaluation and are aligned with the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for SSI prevention. Timely and targeted evaluation and feedback often drive actions related to the other four components of the multimodal strategy. Planning for evaluation and feedback should primarily involve the infection prevention and control (IPC) team and eventually engage all relevant stakeholders to foster an understanding of the importance of local data. Knowledge of the local situation, derived from data and other information, is critical for creating situational awareness and encouraging teamwork. Selecting appropriate process, infrastructure, and knowledge indicators to reflect system and practice changes is a key element that requires the expertise of the IPC team. Furthermore, SSI surveillance is a critical component of the assessment framework for any SSI improvement program. Surveillance data are vital for driving improvements and can be a persuasive tool when clinicians are resistant to change. Conducting monitoring and surveillance activities requires the support and agreement of facility leadership and the heads of targeted surgical services, as these efforts are linked to patient safety and performance assessment. Additional resources, such as dedicated time for trained staff and microbiological investigations, may also be necessary. Building capacity for monitoring and surveillance will require training for the designated surveillance lead (likely the IPC lead) and those responsible for data collection, such as nurses and physicians working in wards or departments where surveillance is conducted. If this expertise is not yet available, developing it should be a priority. Facilities should ask themselves key questions, such as: What are the key processes we want to monitor, and how will we do so? Do we have staff competent in monitoring and providing feedback? Do we have the necessary resources to conduct monitoring? Are there forums where feedback can be delivered? Is the organization prepared to receive and act on feedback? Have staff been asked how they can contribute to improvements following evaluation and feedback? Targeted feedback is a crucial part of driving improvement and behavior change. Facilities should consult and agree on different formats for providing feedback to various staff groups. For example, if the use of alcohol-based antiseptic solutions containing chlorhexidine gluconate for surgical site skin preparation is a planned objective, monitoring preoperative skin disinfection and providing feedback on interim results should be organized. Similarly, if improving surgical hand preparation is a goal, assessing the use of appropriate products and techniques, along with feedback on compliance observations, should be implemented. If avoiding hair removal (or using clippers when absolutely necessary) is a planned objective, monitoring this practice during the preoperative period in the ward or operating room, along with feedback on interim results, should be organized. For objectives such as ensuring correct surgical antibiotic prophylaxis (SAP) administration within two hours before incision, monitoring antibiotic administration and providing feedback on interim results is essential. Roles and responsibilities, including coordination activities, must be clearly defined from the outset. Addressing SSI prevention risk factors requires the involvement of all individuals working in or associated with surgery at different stages of evaluation, feedback, and action planning. For example, if a recommendation is not being adhered to, those directly involved in the associated care should be targeted for monitoring and feedback. Processes or changes in processes are more likely to be integrated into daily practice when staff are actively involved. Locally gathered data from evaluation and feedback efforts can also be incorporated into interactive discussions during training sessions to provide a coherent and motivational approach to driving change. A checklist of actions for evaluation and feedback includes ensuring visible commitment from management, allocating a budget for necessary resources, forming a dedicated and competent monitoring team, developing reliable protocols and indicators, and creating an action plan for monitoring and feedback. Training observers, analyzing data, and using the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist are also critical steps. Facility documentation, such as policies and procurement plans, should align with monitoring indicators. Reminders and workplace communications are key to raising awareness and prompting health workers to follow evidence-based practices for SSI prevention. These reminders should be strategically placed to capture staff attention and emphasize critical actions. Communication strategies should align with training and education materials and be tailored to the local context and culture. Facilities should ask themselves questions such as: Where should reminders be placed, and which recommendations should be targeted? Which staff members would benefit from reminders? What are the key messages to communicate in simple, locally understandable language? Do we have the expertise and resources to develop impactful communications? Have staff been asked how they can contribute to communication efforts? An institutional safety climate and culture are foundational for implementing and sustaining improvements in SSI prevention. This involves creating an environment that prioritizes surgical safety and fosters accountability, advocacy, and teamwork among health workers. Senior clinical leaders and management must visibly support these efforts, and staff should feel safe raising concerns about patient safety. Facilities should assess their safety culture through surveys and develop action plans for change with clear timelines for review. Training opportunities should align with the desired cultural shift. In summary, successful SSI prevention requires a multimodal approach involving monitoring, feedback, communication, and fostering a safety culture. Engaging all relevant staff, ensuring management support, and aligning resources and training with improvement goals are critical to achieving sustainable change.
